reception.text: The bird reservations drew little national press but real gratitude from the young Audubon societies that had lobbied for them.

political_impact.text: The government of the day made no count of the reservations' acreage; a 1912 Biological Survey list noted that most were unsurveyed and their area uncertain.
The routine personnel and land orders of these weeks drew no recorded notice.

legacy.text: The Klamath and Malheur reservations belong to the 51 bird reservations of Roosevelt's presidency, the beginnings of what became the National Wildlife Refuge System.
legacy.source: Palmer, Biological Survey Circular No. 87 (1912), pp. 9–10; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

legacy.text: Key West survives as a national wildlife refuge of about 209,000 acres, nearly all of it open water, taking in the Marquesas Keys and 13 other islands across 375 square miles.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands (as of Sept. 30, 2025)

today.name: Key West National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: 208,937.33 total acres, of which 206,289 are held under agreement or lease, essentially open water.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands (as of Sept. 30, 2025)

today.name: Florida Keys Wilderness
today.note: Key West's share is 2,019 acres; the wilderness also spans the National Key Deer and Great White Heron refuges.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands, Table 8; Pub. L. 93-632

later_actions.text: Congress designated 2,019 acres of the Key West refuge as part of the Florida Keys Wilderness.

related.note: The Florida reservations extended the Gulf Coast chain begun at Pelican Island in 1903.

uncertain: Which refuge complex manages the Key West refuge today should be confirmed; it has been placed in the J. N. "Ding" Darling complex, but the Fish and Wildlife Service also describes it in its Florida Keys complex materials.

political_impact.text: The order made the reservation subject to use by the Reclamation Service under the Reclamation Act of 1902, conceding the reclamation claim in the document that created the refuge.

legacy.text: The Klamath Water Users Association persuaded Woodrow Wilson to cut the Lower Klamath reservation in 1915.
Biological Survey reports of 1916, 1918 and 1919 record homestead applications rejected inside the boundary and organized movements to drain the water from both the Klamath and Malheur reservations.
legacy.source: Bureau of Biological Survey, annual reports, 1916, 1918, 1919

legacy.text: Four later executive orders took the reservation from a reconstructed 81,619 acres down to 46,902 as reclamation drained much of Lower Klamath Lake.
legacy.source: Klamath Basin NWR Complex Final CCP/EIS (Dec. 2016), App. G; research entry

legacy.text: The Fish and Wildlife Service calls Lower Klamath the nation's first waterfowl refuge; that framing is the agency's, since the 1908 order uses the same "native birds" language as every order in the series.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; EO 924

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2200 reduced the reservation, after the Klamath Water Users Association pressed its case with Wilson.
Executive Order 3187 reduced the reservation further.
Executive Order 3422 reduced the reservation further.
Executive Order 8475 revoked the 1908 order as to a single lot of 7.80 acres.

related.note: The Oregon Audubon Society pressed for both the Klamath and Malheur reservations.

political_impact.text: By 1911 questions had arisen with residents of adjoining land over cutting hay, burning tules, grazing hogs, destroying coyotes and trapping; the Biological Survey reported meeting them so as to keep friendly relations.
political_impact.source: Bureau of Biological Survey, annual report, 1911

political_impact.text: The Biological Survey's 1912 list numbered Lake Malheur 19th among the national bird reservations.
political_impact.source: Palmer, Biological Survey Circular No. 87 (1912), pp. 9–10

legacy.text: Oregon claimed title to Malheur Lake in 1916, a fight settled only by the Supreme Court in 1935, which described the reservation as 81,786 acres of unsurveyed land within a 105.36-mile meander line.
Biological Survey reports of 1916, 1918 and 1919 record organized movements to drain the water from both the Klamath and Malheur reservations.
legacy.source: Bureau of Biological Survey, annual reports, 1916, 1918, 1919

legacy.text: The refuge grew to more than twice its 1908 size with the Blitzen Valley addition of 1935 and the Double-O Unit of 1941.
In 2016 an armed group occupied the refuge headquarters in a standoff over federal control of Western land.

today.name: Malheur National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: 187,171.20 acres as of September 30, 2025; one of the largest freshwater marsh and wetland refuges in the West.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands (as of Sept. 30, 2025), Table 3

later_actions.text: The Supreme Court settled Oregon's claim to Malheur Lake in United States v. Oregon.
The Blitzen Valley was added to the refuge.
The Double-O Unit was added to the refuge.

related.note: The Oregon Audubon Society pressed for both reservations.

political_impact.text: The Biological Survey's 1912 list numbered Chase Lake 20th among the national bird reservations.
political_impact.source: Palmer, Biological Survey Circular No. 87 (1912), pp. 9–10

legacy.text: Chase Lake remains a refuge that has at times hosted nearly a third of the continental white-pelican population, in the Fish and Wildlife Service's words.

today.name: Chase Lake National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: 4,385 acres; managed in the Eastern North Dakota refuge complex.

later_actions.text: A 4,155-acre wilderness was designated within the refuge.

today.name: Pine Island National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: 608.48 acres; part of the J. N. "Ding" Darling refuge complex.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands (as of Sept. 30, 2025)

related.note: The Florida reservations extended the Gulf Coast chain begun at Pelican Island in 1903.

legacy.text: The reservation was renamed the Palma Sola National Wildlife Refuge in 1940 and revoked in 1948; the revoking order describes a small unsurveyed island of about two acres.

today.name: Palma Sola National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: Revoked in 1948; the land reverted to the public-land laws on April 9, 1948.

later_actions.text: Renamed the Palma Sola National Wildlife Refuge by Proclamation 2416.
Public Land Order 446 revoked Executive Order 942; the island reverted to the public-land laws on April 9, 1948.

related.note: The Florida reservations extended the Gulf Coast chain begun at Pelican Island in 1903.

uncertain: Why the reservation was revoked in 1948 is not known; the revoking order gives no reason, and an unsourced story that the island eroded away may confuse it with Passage Key.
The size of the reservation in 1908 is not known; the two-acre figure is from the 1948 revocation.

today.name: Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: Has "grown to 31 islands encompassing over 500 acres" (564.73 acres as of Sept. 30, 2025); part of the J. N. "Ding" Darling refuge complex.
today.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Annual Report of Lands (as of Sept. 30, 2025)

related.note: The Florida reservations extended the Gulf Coast chain begun at Pelican Island in 1903.

uncertain: The later history of this Fort Bayard watershed withdrawal has not been traced.
The later history of the Tanana Signal Corps reservation has not been traced.
The later history of the Belle Fourche experiment-farm reservation has not been traced. It is not the Belle Fourche bird reservation, which came later by Executive Order 1032.
The later history of the Circle wireless-station reservation has not been traced.
